name: Masai
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Tucker, A. N. & Mpaayei, J. T. Ole (1955) A Maasai Grammar with Vocabulary. Longmans (Maasai described as tonal; grammar plausibly states accent/prosody)

new_statements.quote: In most words all syllables are accentuated alike, a very slight stress being perhaps laid on the penultimate. This is more particularly noticeable when the last syllable but one contains a long vowel, e. g. ol-ayóni, 'n-joníto. Should the accent fall on any other syllable but the penultimate, it is specially marked, thus: ol-móruo, kewárie. [p. 8:] The accent, such as it is, does not fall on the penultimate in the following cases: I. When the subject of a verb is the first person plural, the last syllable is always slightly accentuated. [...] II. Whenever one of two a's falls out before i in verbs commencing with the latter letter, the remaining a is rather more strongly sounded than the other syllables
new_statements.citation: Hollis, A. C. (1905). The Masai: Their Language and Folklore. Oxford: Clarendon Press. Section 'The Accent', pp. 7-9.
new_statements.locator: pp. 7-8 (section 'The Accent'; PDF pages 43-44 of the archive.org scan)
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is weak and nearly level across syllables; where perceptible it tends to the penultimate syllable, most clearly when the penult vowel is long. Words with non-penultimate accent are marked individually in the book (ol-móruo, kewárie). The same pages then describe raising/lowering of the voice at word end as the invariable marker of subject vs object (an early observation of Maa grammatical tone), so the book treats pitch, not stress, as the contrastive prosody.
new_statements.exceptions: (I) verbs with 1st-person-plural subject take slight final-syllable stress (ki-súj, ki-tu-suj-á); (II) when aa- contracts to a- before i-initial verb stems the surviving a is more strongly sounded (á-isuj-a); lexical items marked with non-penultimate accent (ol-móruo, kewárie). Note that Hinde 1901 (p. 2, also saved) gives a conflicting impressionistic rule: accent usually on the first syllable of disyllables, otherwise mostly the second syllable, 'not very regular', some words with all syllables equal.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms of nouns and inflected verbs; the p. 8 voice raising/lowering rule concerns word-final pitch in the sentence (subject vs object marking).
new_statements.identity_note: Hollis 1905 and Hinde 1901 describe the Maasai of British East Africa (Kenya; Hollis distinguishes 'Northern' and 'Southern' Masai forms), i.e. language-level masa1300. Karani 2018 (silent on stress) describes the Parakuyo dialect of Tanzania; Levergood 1987 (not opened) describes Arusa (Arusha), also a Maa dialect. Modern sources (Payne; WALS 13A) treat Maa as a two-tone (H/L) language.

sources.note: Section 'The Accent' pp. 7-9: all syllables accentuated nearly alike, very slight stress on the penultimate (clearest with a long penult vowel); non-penult accent marked lexically; final stress in 1pl-subject verbs and on contracted a- in a-i- verbs; subject/object distinguished by raising/lowering the voice at word end. Verified against the page image.

sources.citation: Hinde, Hildegarde (1901). The Masai Language: Grammatical Notes together with a Vocabulary. Cambridge: University Press.
sources.note: p. 2 (verified on page image): 'The accent in Masai usually falls on the first syllable in words of two syllables, and in words of two or three syllables most usually on the second, but occasionally on the third. In words of more than three syllables the accent is usually on the second syllable. The accentuation is, however, not very regular, and in some words all the syllables are of equal value.' Preface p. v: the name Masai itself has 'the accent very markedly on the first syllable'. Non-linguist author; impressionistic.

sources.citation: Karani, Michael (2018). Syntactic categories and argument structure in Parakuyo-Maasai. PhD dissertation, Stellenbosch University.
sources.note: Section 2.2 'Parakuyo phonology' (pp. 15-22) covers vowels, consonants, syllable structure and tone (two contrastive tones H and L, case marked by tone, following Tucker & Mpaayei 1955 and Payne 2012); no mention of stress or accent anywhere in the dissertation (grep of full text).
